1128.title: Lady Poverty
1128.hook: Francis spoke of poverty as a bride: freedom from owning
1128.howItsDone: Franciscan friars and sisters take a vow of poverty and hold possessions in common; lay Franciscans and other Christians inspired by Francis practice simplicity and giving in ordinary life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, heaven on earth: a room fuller than it looks. Your line was heaven is near.

A young man stands before the bishop in Assisi, a hill town in Italy. His father, a cloth merchant, is furious: the son has been giving away money and goods the father counts as his. So the son does something nobody there expects. He hands back the money, then takes off his very clothes and hands those back too. From now on, the early accounts have him say, he'll call only God his father. The bishop wraps his own cloak around him. The young man is Francis; you met him back on day eight hundred fourteen. And he's about to fall in love with someone unexpected. Today's word: Lady Poverty.

Francis spoke about poverty the way a knight in an old love song speaks of his lady: poverty was his bride, and he courted her. One early allegory turns it into a story. Francis and his brothers climb a mountain to find Lady Poverty, and bring her down to share a meal: a little bread and cold water. When she asks to see their cloister, they lead her to a hilltop and show her the whole world. This, they say, is our cloister. Why a bride, and not a burden? Because for Francis, poverty meant freedom. Things own you back. A house wants guarding, money wants counting, a fine coat wants protecting from the rain. He heard the Gospel words where Jesus sends out his disciples, "Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses," and tradition says he took them at face value. He looked at Jesus himself: "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Owning nothing left Francis's hands free: for lepers, for the poor, for praise. A careful word here. Nothing in his story makes forced hunger holy. In the early accounts, Francis chooses to share the life of the poor and stand beside them, and gives away what comes to him. Christians take his example in different ways. Franciscan friars and sisters still take vows of poverty. Others hear it as a question to carry: how much is enough, and what do my things ask of me?

Walk through your home in your mind, a closet, a shelf, a drawer, and find one thing you don't need that someone else could use: not the thing you'd never miss, but one with a little pull to it. Hold it in mind and notice the tug; that pull is what Francis wanted to be free of. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
Lady Poverty. Francis's name for the life of owning nothing, loved like a bride because it set him free.
Your line: free of things. What you own can own you back. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1129.title: Perfect joy
1129.hook: Francis says perfect joy is being turned away cold and wet and staying patient (Little Flowers 8)
1129.howItsDone: Franciscans and other Christians tell the story of perfect joy from the Little Flowers of St Francis as a lesson in humility and patience; the story itself ends with Paul's words about glorying only in the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lady Poverty: Francis's bride, and freedom from owning. Your line was free of things.

Winter. Two friars walk a long road in bitter cold, Brother Leo out in front and Francis behind. Francis calls ahead. Brother Leo, write this down. If our brothers everywhere set a great example of holiness, that is not perfect joy. He calls again. If a brother healed the sick and gave sight to the blind, write it down: that is not perfect joy. If he knew every language and all the scriptures, and could tell the future, not perfect joy. If he preached so well that unbelievers turned to God, not perfect joy. At last Leo, amazed, asks: Father, then what is perfect joy?

Francis answers with a scene. We arrive at our own friary at night, soaked with rain, stiff with cold, spattered with mud and hungry, and we knock at the gate. The brother on the door says, Who are you? We say, two of your brothers. And he says, You're lying. You're a pair of tramps who go around fooling people and taking the alms of the poor. Go away. And he leaves us outside in the snow and the rain. If we bear that patiently, without grumbling, and think that perhaps this porter knows us as we truly are, write it down, Brother Leo: that is perfect joy. The story pushes further: they knock again and are driven off; again, and are beaten. Still, perfect joy. Why? Everything on his first list is God's gift, so nobody can boast of it. He quotes Paul: "what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" The one thing a person can bring of their own is to bear a hard thing patiently, for love of Christ. And Paul again: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." This isn't a call to stay in harm's way. It's a story about pride. The usual move is to rehearse the speech: do you know who I am? Francis's joy is not needing to win that argument. Yesterday he was free of things. Today he's free of his own reputation.
screen: `NOTHING OF OUR OWN TO BOAST OF.`

segments.voice: Recall a recent time you were brushed off, a message ignored, a flat no, someone who didn't believe you, and notice the old speech start up: the defense, the comeback. Don't deliver it; let it run out, like rain off a roof. If you pray, hold that moment before God; if you don't, just breathe, and let the door stay shut. And if someone is truly hurting you, this isn't a door to wait at: please reach someone you trust, or local emergency help.
Perfect joy. Francis's name for bearing a hard rejection patiently, for love, with nothing to prove.
Your line: perfect joy. Nothing to prove, nothing to win. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

1130.title: Brother and sister creatures
1130.howItsDone: Christians sing or pray Francis's Canticle of the Creatures, sometimes in hymn versions, and some churches bless animals on or near his feast day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, perfect joy: shut out in the snow, and patient. Your line was perfect joy.

Laudato si', mi' Signore. Praised be you, my Lord. That's the refrain of a song Francis made in the everyday Italian of his own region; you first heard it on day two hundred sixty-nine. Tradition says he made it late in life, when he was ill and could hardly see. It's called the Canticle of the Creatures, or the Canticle of Brother Sun, and it does something unusual. It doesn't just list the sun among God's works. It calls him Brother Sun. Then Sister Moon and the stars. Brother Wind. Sister Water. Brother Fire. Sister, and Mother, Earth. Every creature he names, he names as family.

Listen to how he describes them. Sister Water is useful and humble and precious and pure. Brother Fire is beautiful and cheerful, strong, and lights up the night. Sister Mother Earth feeds us, and brings out fruit and colored flowers and grass. Each gets a small portrait, as if Francis knew them personally. And the little word in each line, per, can be heard more than one way: praised be you for Brother Sun, or by him, or through him. Readers take it differently, and the song may hold all three. The Bible already has creation singing. Psalm one hundred forty-eight calls on everything to praise: "Praise ye him, sun and moon: praise him, all ye stars of light." Francis takes one step further and gives them family names. The Little Flowers has stories to match. Francis preaches to a crowd of birds, telling them to thank God for their feathers and the air, and they stay to listen. Near the town of Gubbio a wolf has been terrifying the people. Francis goes out to meet him, calls him Brother Wolf, and makes peace: the wolf stops attacking, and the town agrees to feed him. Then, tradition says, near the very end Francis added one more verse, for one more relative: Sister Bodily Death, whom no one living can escape. Even she is family. If the sun, the wolf and even death are your siblings, nothing in the world is just a thing.

Bring to mind one creature you've met today: a dog, a tree outside the window, the water in your glass, the sun on the floor. Give it Francis's kind of name, Brother Tree, Sister Water, and notice what it does for you without being asked. Then thank it, silently or out loud; if you pray, you can praise God through it, the way the Canticle does.
Brother and sister creatures. Francis's way of seeing sun, water, wolf and even death as family, in one household of praise.
Your line: family of creation. In Francis's song, even the water in your glass is kin. Until tomorrow.

1131.title: Make me an instrument
1131.hook: the prayer called Francis's comes from long after him, but carries his spirit
1131.howItsDone: Christians in a range of churches pray the Peace Prayer, known as the Prayer of Saint Francis, alone or together, and it is also sung as a hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, brother and sister creatures: sun, water, wolf, even death, all family. Your line was family of creation.

There's a prayer that turns up on cards, on kitchen walls, on the backs of service sheets, sometimes printed with a name underneath: Saint Francis. It begins by asking to be made an instrument of peace. Here's the surprise. It isn't found in anything from Francis's own time. Those who've traced it find it long after him, in French, in a small church publication, with no author's name at all. Somewhere along the way it picked up his name and kept it. So why does it carry his name so easily? Some readers say it's because it sounds like him.
screen: `A PRAYER WITH HIS NAME ON IT.`

segments.voice: The prayer is built in two halves. The first is a list of swaps. Where there's hatred, it asks to bring love. Where there's injury, pardon. Then doubt and faith, despair and hope, darkness and light, sadness and joy. Each line asks to carry into a room the opposite of what's already in it. The second half turns the usual wish around: not so much to be consoled as to console, to be understood as to understand, to be loved as to love. It ends with reversals that sound like the Gospel: it is in giving that we receive, in pardoning that we are pardoned, in dying that we are born to eternal life. Now the word instrument. Paul uses it in his letter to the Romans: "yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God." An instrument doesn't play itself. A violin doesn't pick the tune; it only has to be in tune, and in the right hands. That's the humility here. The prayer doesn't promise to make peace by sheer effort. It asks to be used. And Jesus blessed exactly that work: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." So does it matter that Francis didn't write it? Set it beside this week: the clothes handed back, the cold gate borne patiently, the wolf called brother. Written far from Assisi, long after him, it still lets some readers hear his voice. A prayer can carry a saint's spirit without carrying his signature.

If you know the prayer and you pray, say it once, slowly, letting each pair land before the next; if you pray but don't know it, take Jesus's line instead: blessed are the peacemakers. If you don't pray, choose one pair from the list, hatred and love, despair and hope, and sit with one place in your life where that swap is needed.
Make me an instrument. The opening request of the peace prayer that carries Francis's name: not to do great things, but to be used for peace.
Your line: an instrument of peace. A violin only has to be in tune. Same time tomorrow.

1132.title: Preach always
1132.hook: Franciscans are known for serving before speaking
1132.howItsDone: Franciscan friars and sisters, and lay people who follow Francis's way, often serve the poor and the sick in quiet, practical ways, and speak of letting their lives bear witness alongside their words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prayer that carries Francis's spirit: make me an instrument. Your line was an instrument of peace.

A rule for a band of brothers has a chapter on preaching. It opens with a warning: no brother is to preach against the Church's ways, or without his minister's permission. So far, a rule about who may stand up and speak. Then comes one short line that widens the whole chapter: all the brothers, though, should preach by their works. Not some of them. All of them. The cook, the one mending a roof, the one sitting up with a sick man. The rule is the one Francis of Assisi gave his first brothers, and in that line nobody is left out of preaching.

Francis didn't invent the idea. He found it in the Gospel. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus says: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." Notice who gets the glory: not the one shining. The light points away from itself. The letter of James puts it with a shrug: "shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works." Words can say faith. Works show it. And the first letter of John says it tenderly: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." That's the ground Francis stood on. In the stories told about him and his first brothers, they work with their hands, they look after lepers, they sweep out churches. When they do speak, the speaking comes out of a life people have already watched. Now, a fair word for the other side. The early stories have Francis preaching out loud too, in town squares as well as churches. And Paul asks how anyone will believe in one of whom they have not heard. So, in this way of reading it, it isn't works instead of words. It's an order of things. The life comes first and stays longest; words, when they come, have somewhere to stand. A sermon ends. A life is preached every day, including the days you'd rather nobody was watching.
screen: `SHEW ME THY FAITH BY MY WORKS.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind who could use a hand, a tired coworker, a neighbor, someone at home, and find one small thing for them: wash what they'd have to wash, refill what's empty, carry what's heavy. Then settle the harder part: no hint, no credit. If you pray, you can offer it to God in advance.
Preach always. The heart of a line in Francis's rule: let all the brothers preach by their works, so the life speaks before the mouth does.
Your line: preach with your life. The light points away from itself. See you tomorrow.

1133.title: Carmel
1133.hook: the Carmelites trace their spirit to Elijah on Mount Carmel
1133.tomorrow: Four ways to water a garden
1133.howItsDone: Carmelite friars and nuns keep long periods of silent prayer each day, often alone in a cell or together in chapel, and look to Elijah as a father of their way of life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis's rule: preach by your works. Your line was preach with your life.

A ridge of hills called Carmel runs down toward the sea in the north of Israel. In the First Book of Kings, this is where the prophet Elijah calls down fire: an altar, a trench full of water, a crowd waiting, and then fire falls and burns up everything, even the water. Centuries later, tradition says, Christian hermits settled on that same mountain, in small cells near a spring people connected with Elijah. They became the Carmelites. And the spirit they took from Elijah isn't only the fire. It's also what happened to him next, after he ran.

Right after the fire, Elijah is running for his life. The queen has sworn to kill him. He walks into the wilderness, sits under a bush, and asks to die. An angel wakes him twice with bread and water, and he walks on to Horeb, the mountain of God, and hides in a cave. Then God says, go out and stand on the mountain. The King James tells it: "a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice." The prophet who called down fire learns that God isn't in this fire. Hearing the quiet, Elijah wraps his face in his cloak and goes to the mouth of the cave. That's the turn the Carmelites took as theirs. Carmel is the fire. Horeb is the whisper. A Carmelite life holds both: zeal for God, and long hours of silent prayer in a small room, listening. The Hebrew behind still small voice is hard to put into English: some hear a gentle whisper, others a sound made of thin silence. God, in this story, chooses to be found in a hush, by a man worn out and hiding. And the voice asks the question he first heard in the cave: what are you doing here, Elijah?
screen: `NOT IN THE WIND, QUAKE OR FIRE.`
`AFTER THE FIRE, A STILL SMALL VOICE.`

segments.voice: Let the noise come first, worries like wind, something unfinished like a quake, anger like fire, and let each pass; you don't have to make the quiet, only wait for it. If you pray, wait for God as Elijah did, face covered; if not, listen for the smallest sound in the room. And if, like Elijah under that bush, you ever feel you'd rather not be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Carmel. Elijah's mountain of fire, home of the first Carmelites, who carried his quieter lesson too.
Your line: the still small voice. After the fire comes the hush, and a question. Until tomorrow.

1134.title: Four ways to water a garden
1134.word: Four ways to water a garden
1134.hook: Teresa: prayer can be like carrying buckets, a water wheel, a stream, or rain
1134.howItsDone: Teresa's image of the four waters is taught in Carmelite houses and retreats as a way to describe the growth of prayer, from effortful meditation toward quieter prayer received as gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carmel, and Elijah on Horeb, where God wasn't in the wind or the fire. Your line was the still small voice.

A Carmelite nun in Spain is asked by her confessors to write down how she prays. Her name is Teresa, from the city of Ávila. She isn't a trained theologian, and she says so. So instead of a system, she reaches for a garden. Someone is handed a patch of hard, weedy ground and told to make it grow. In her account, the Lord has already pulled up the weeds and put in good plants. The job left is water. And there are, she says, four ways to get it there.

First: you draw water from a well by hand and carry it in buckets. Heavy, slow, and some days the well seems dry. Teresa says this is how prayer often begins: effort, attention, gathering a wandering mind, again and again. Second: a water wheel, turned by a crank, lifting many buckets at once. Less sweat, more water. Prayer grows quieter; the soul rests a little, and something is given that you didn't haul up yourself. Third: a stream running through the garden. Now the gardener mostly guides where the water goes. Fourth: rain. The gardener does nothing at all. As the ways go on, the gardener works less and the Lord gives more. Teresa doesn't call the buckets a failure. They're where she says people begin, and she's frank that she spent long, dry years there herself. Back on day one hundred six, a dry prayer still counted; her buckets are that same dry work. She doesn't promise the steps come in a neat line, either. The garden can go back to buckets. Psalm sixty-five has a line for her fourth way: "Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it." And Paul, of his own work: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." This has been a week of letting go: Lady Poverty, perfect joy in the cold, brother sun and sister water, an instrument of peace, a life that preaches, Elijah in the hush. Teresa adds her own: keep carrying the bucket, and leave the rain to God.
screen: `THE GARDENER WORKS LESS, GOD GIVES MORE.`

segments.voice: Ask honestly which picture fits your prayer, or your inner life, right now: buckets, hard work and not much coming up; a wheel, some rhythm; a stream, things moving on their own; or rain, something given you didn't earn. There's no right answer and no grade, so just name it. If you pray, you can tell God which one it is today; if you don't, simply notice the dry places and the wet ones.
Four ways to water a garden. Teresa of Ávila's picture of prayer: buckets, a wheel, a stream, and rain, with less of our work and more of God's as it goes.
screen: `FOUR WAYS TO WATER A GARDEN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: sometimes buckets, sometimes rain. Hauling water is no proof you're doing it wrong. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

chat.says: Prayer has felt like hard work for me lately. Am I doing it wrong?
options: Not necessarily. Teresa says many begin with buckets, and she spent long, dry years there herself.
Probably. Teresa teaches that real prayer feels effortless from the very first day.
Yes. If it's hard, God isn't listening, so you should wait until it feels easy.
